data.agents#Coding agents:
Since v0.7.0 the gateway serves the three APIs coding tools speak, in front of the cluster’s own models. Every request authenticates with a virtual key as the bearer token and goes through the same budgets, guardrails and fair-share priority, so an agent’s consumption lands in its team’s share.
Tool speaks Route Notes OpenAI chat completions POST /v1/chat/completions the default for editors such as VS Code with Continue OpenAI Responses POST /v1/responses stateless only: no previous_response_id, no stored responses Anthropic Messages POST /v1/messages vLLM’s native Anthropic endpoint, no translation in the gateway
data.anthropic#Agents that speak the Anthropi:
POST /v1/messages lets an agent that speaks the Messages API use a local model. The gateway’s README says to point such an agent at the gateway “with a virtual key as the bearer token”. The request shape is the Messages API’s:
curl https://llm.example.org/v1/messages \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $LLMFLOW_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model": "llama-3.3-70b", "max_tokens": 256, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]}' How a given agent is told its base URL and its key (an environment variable, a settings file) is that agent’s own configuration, which this site does not reproduce: read it in the agent’s documentation.
What the gateway guarantees on this route: guardrails cover system, text and thinking blocks, tool_result content and the strings inside tool_use inputs; guarded streams pass through an Anthropic event filter; error bodies carry "type": "error"; /v1/messages/count_tokens is not routed. Accounting counts cached tokens as vLLM reports them.
data.continue#VS Code with Continue:
Continue is configured for the gateway exactly as for any OpenAI-compatible server; the file and its keys are on the VS Code page, taken from Continue’s own documentation. Point apiBase at the gateway’s /v1 and use the user’s virtual key. Whether a given Continue version can call /v1/responses is a question for Continue’s documentation, which this site has not opened for that route: the safe choice is /v1/chat/completions.
A request through /v1/chat/completions that the gateway accepts, whatever the client:
curl https://llm.example.org/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $LLMFLOW_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model": "llama-3.3-70b", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]}'
data.limits#Limits to keep in mind: A Responses stream under post-call guardrails is refused: ask with "stream": false. A guarded stream that carries tool-call arguments in the chat API is stopped; ask without stream. A client chat_template is stripped, and so are priority, extra_body and the other engine fields. The performance of the current release is not measured yet.
data.responses#The Responses API, and why it:
A client that uses /v1/responses must send the whole conversation in input each time. The gateway forces "store": false and answers 400 to previous_response_id, background, conversation and a stored prompt:
curl https://llm.example.org/v1/responses \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $LLMFLOW_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model": "llama-3.3-70b", "input": "Hello"}' Why. vLLM keeps stored responses in the memory of the instance that produced them, readable and continuable by anyone who holds the id. On a shared cluster, a tenant holding an id could read or continue another tenant’s conversation, so the gateway does not allow state. GET /v1/responses/{id} and the cancel route are not routed.

data.alerts#Alerts: Soft-budget alerts are retried with exponential backoff, up to 6 attempts, and every webhook attempt carries the same Idempotency-Key so that a receiver can de-duplicate. Retries live in memory: a gateway stopped mid-retry does not resume.
data.anchors#Anchors: Every checkpoint, and the entries it covers, is also written to the anchor export (audit/checkpoints/.json, audit/entries/-.jsonl.gz). On S3 the objects go under Object Lock retention when the bucket has it enabled; create the bucket that way, since MinIO and Ceph RGW require it at creation, with versioning. A file export refuses to overwrite a file but does not stop its owner. The age of the newest exported checkpoint is the metric llmflow_audit_anchor_age_seconds, and a checkpoint still unexported after anchor_max_lag raises the alert audit_anchor_lag.
data.audit#Audit and logging: v0.5.0 of the gateway (roadmap milestone M3) answers three questions: who changed what in the administration, can that record be trusted, and what may be kept about the requests themselves. This page is written from the gateway’s README at that tag; where the guarantees end is stated as plainly as where they hold.
data.configuration#A configuration:
This was run through llmflow-gateway check-config v0.8.0, with the key files present and a configuration (organisations, a pool and a model) around it.
store { kind = "postgres" dsn_file = "/etc/llmflow/pg.dsn" } audit { signing_key_file = "/etc/llmflow/audit.seed" checkpoint_interval = "5m" anchor = "archive" anchor_max_lag = "15m" retention = { admin = "61320h", auth = "8760h", scim = "8760h", system = "8760h" } prune_interval = "24h" } export "archive" { kind = "s3" endpoint = "https://minio.example.org:9000" bucket = "llmflow-audit" path_style = true access_key_file = "/etc/llmflow/s3.access" secret_key_file = "/etc/llmflow/s3.secret" prefix = "gateway-1/" lock_mode = "COMPLIANCE" retention = "8760h" queue_size = 1024 } logging "research" { teams = ["lab-nlp", "lab-chem"] destination = "archive" content = false max_content_bytes = 1048576 batch_records = 500 batch_interval = "1m" lock = false } policy "attributed" { teams = ["lab-nlp"] require = ["user", "metadata.project"] require_tags = true } policy "long-context" { max_body_bytes = 33554432 max_response_bytes = 134217728 } The signing_key_file is an Ed25519 seed, made with llmflow-gateway audit keygen -o FILE. Like every *_file attribute it may be a vault: reference instead of a path.
data.exports#Export targets: kind is s3 or file. gcs and azure answer “not implemented”. The S3 client is go-volumes/s3. Exports go through a bounded queue; a batch dropped or given up is counted and alerted (export_dropped, export_failed), never silent.
data.log#The admin audit log:
Every state-changing admin request is recorded, accepted or refused: the actor and their roles, the action, the target, the state before and after, the request body, the status, the client address and a request id. Events the gateway raises itself go to the same log: SSO logins and logouts, key rotations, SCIM reconciliation. Key secrets and tokens never appear, and reads are not audited.
The log is append-only in PostgreSQL (a trigger refuses UPDATE) and hash-chained: each entry stores a SHA-256 of the previous hash and itself, so altering, inserting, reordering or deleting an entry breaks every hash after it. With a signing key, checkpoints sign the newest hash at an interval and at shutdown.
data.policies#Request policies:
A policy refuses inference requests that lack given fields, and replaces the global size limits, for the teams it names and for keys created with it (POST /admin/keys {"policy": "..."}, by a team admin; a key’s own policy wins over its team’s).
require lists body fields (a name or a dotted path); require_tags = true asks for at least one request tag. A refused request gets a 400 naming what is missing, and counts in llmflow_denied_total{reason="policy"}. max_body_bytes and max_response_bytes replace the global limits. The response limit is not applied to streams.
data.request-logs#Per-team request logs:
By default no request log is written for anyone: the spend metadata goes to the accounting store; prompts and completions are forwarded and forgotten, and the gateway’s own log never holds them.
A logging block sends the requests of the teams it names to an export. Each request is one JSON line (time, org, team, project, key id, model, pool, upstream, tokens, cost, latency, status, priority, borrowing, stream, estimated, tags, request id). Content is off: only a block with content = true, an explicit opt-in, adds the request and the answer, each cut at max_content_bytes and marked request_truncated or response_truncated. A team is in at most one block. Lines are batched into gzipped objects under requests//YYYY/MM/DD/.
data.retention#Retention: Entries are kept for ever unless a retention is set per kind (admin, auth for SSO, scim, system). Every prune_interval the gateway deletes the longest prefix of the log that ends at a signed checkpoint and whose every entry is past its kind’s retention: whole segments only, so what remains starts from a signed checkpoint and still verifies. A kind without a retention stops the cut. It never prunes past the newest checkpoint the anchor holds, and never a log that does not verify (audit_prune_refused is raised instead). Each prune is itself an audit.pruned entry.
data.threat-model#What this protects against: Without an anchor With an anchor kept outside an entry edited, inserted, reordered or deleted in the middle detected detected the tail deleted together with the checkpoints that cover it not detected detected an older consistent backup restored (rollback) not detected detected everything deleted not detected detected a log rewritten and re-signed with a stolen key, up to the anchor not detected detected entries after the newest exported checkpoint deleted not detected still open: at most checkpoint_interval plus the export lag a new history signed after the anchor by the holder of the signing key not detected still open Entries and checkpoints live in the same database, which is why an anchor outside it is needed. To narrow what stays open, keep the signing key in OpenBao or Vault, verify with a public key kept elsewhere, and anchor on write-once storage.
data.verifying#Verifying: llmflow-gateway audit keygen -o audit.seed # once; keep the seed in Vault llmflow-gateway audit pubkey -c gateway.hcl # the public key, to keep elsewhere llmflow-gateway audit verify -c gateway.hcl --public-key KEY --anchor export llmflow-gateway audit verify -c gateway.hcl --public-key KEY --anchor file:PATH verify recomputes the chain, checks every checkpoint and, with --anchor, checks the database against the newest checkpoint of the export (or of a file you kept yourself). Take the public key from somewhere the gateway’s operator cannot change. Run without an anchor, verify prints a warning, for the reason below.

data.benchmarking#Benchmarking:
The bench repository holds two small command-line tools, in pure Go, for measuring LLM gateways such as the gateway: gwbench measures the latency a gateway adds, and fakevllm is the upstream it is measured against. Repository →
This page is written from the repository’s README at v0.1.0.
go install github.com/go-llmflow/bench/cmd/gwbench@latest go install github.com/go-llmflow/bench/cmd/fakevllm@latest
data.control#The control: TestPlantedOverheadIsMeasured puts a proxy that sleeps a known 3 ms and a transparent proxy in front of a test upstream. The instrument must report about 3 ms for the first and about 0 for the second, and separate the two. If it could not see a planted delay, its verdict on real gateways would mean nothing.
data.example#An example: fakevllm --addr 127.0.0.1:18000 --out /tmp/requests.jsonl & llmflow-gateway serve --config llmflow.hcl & # forwards to 127.0.0.1:18000 gwbench llmflow-key --admin http://127.0.0.1:18080 --master-key-file ~/keys/master --out ~/keys/llmflow gwbench run --direct http://127.0.0.1:18000/v1/chat/completions \ --target 'v0.8.0|http://127.0.0.1:18080/v1/chat/completions|'"$HOME"'/keys/llmflow' \ --rounds 2000 --warmup 200 --runs 8 --wait 2h --max-load 4
data.fakevllm#fakevllm:
fakevllm --addr 127.0.0.1:18000 --out requests.jsonl --model fake --reply "ok" Route Answer GET /v1/models one model, named by --model POST /v1/messages an Anthropic message; with "stream": true, the event sequence message_start, content_block_start, content_block_delta…, content_block_stop, message_delta (with usage.output_tokens), message_stop any other POST an OpenAI chat.completion; with "stream": true, chat.completion.chunk events (role, one chunk per word of --reply, finish), the usage chunk with empty choices when stream_options.include_usage is set, then data: [DONE] Usage is predictable: one prompt token per whitespace-separated word of the request’s message and system strings, and one completion token per word of --reply. --delay and --token-delay slow the answer and the stream.
Every request is appended to --out (mode 0600) as one JSON line, {"method","path","headers","body"}; a body that is not JSON is recorded as a string. The recording holds the headers as received, Authorization included. That is by design, since it is a witness of what a gateway forwarded. Use test keys only. If the record cannot be written, the request gets a 500, so a test never reads a silent gap as “nothing was forwarded”. Bodies are capped by --max-body (1 MiB; larger ones get a 413).
data.interleaving#Interleaving: Each round sends one request to every target, one at a time, in a fresh random order (seeded with --seed). Drift of the machine (thermal state, a background job, the cache) then spreads evenly over all targets instead of penalising whichever runs last. The first --warmup rounds are discarded.
data.keys#Keys: Keys are read from files, never from the command line or the environment. A KEYFILE may be empty for an open endpoint. gwbench llmflow-key creates an llmflow virtual key through the admin API (--master-key-file) and writes it to a file of mode 0600. Keep key files outside the repository.
data.load#Load gating:
Ratios measured on a busy machine are meaningless. A run starts only when the 1-minute load average is at most --max-load (default 4). With --wait, the tool waits for the load to fall; without it, it refuses at once. A run whose load ends above the limit is discarded, not averaged. --runs kept runs are collected, and their rounds stay paired when they are merged.
The load is read from /proc/loadavg on Linux and from sysctl vm.loadavg on macOS. Elsewhere the tool cannot read it and refuses to measure.
data.pairing#Pairing: A gateway’s overhead in round r is its latency minus the direct latency of the same round. Percentiles are taken over these paired differences, which cancels what both paths share: the client, the loopback and the upstream.
data.requests#Requests: Requests are POST chat completions with max_tokens: 1 and one user message: ping, or the content of --prompt-file, sent as a JSON string. An HTTP status other than 200 aborts the run: an error is never timed as a success.
data.result#The result: run 7 kept: load 3.50 -> 3.70 # or: run N discarded: load a -> b kept runs=8, rounds per run=2000, warm-up=200 run 0 overhead p50: v0.1.0=96.125µs v0.6.0=109.999µs ... target p50 p90 p99 # raw latencies, all kept runs direct 81.833µs 93.041µs 138.458µs v0.6.0 193.875µs 212.292µs 351.834µs overhead vs direct, paired per round (all kept runs): v0.6.0 111.042µs 129.541µs 261.624µs # the answer The per-run p50 lines show whether the runs agree; the last table is the result. Report it with the load range of the kept runs, the machine, and the GOMAXPROCS of each gateway.
data.what#What is measured:
The question is “how much latency does a gateway add?”, not “how fast is the model”. The upstream must therefore answer as fast as possible: that is fakevllm, which replies instantly. The number reported is a difference between two paths to the same upstream, not a latency.
direct calls the upstream itself. Every other target (--litellm, --llmflow, or --target NAME|URL|KEYFILE, repeatable) is a gateway forwarding to that same upstream.

data.aborted#Aborted requests: vLLM’s usage chunk comes last. When the client leaves before it, the gateway stops reading (vLLM is not kept generating for nobody) and charges an estimate: prompt bytes / 4 plus the content deltas already forwarded. The record is flagged, in an estimated_requests column of the spend reports and in PostgreSQL. The estimate undercounts tool-call and reasoning tokens.
data.admin-api#Admin API:
Admin routes take Authorization: Bearer or a user’s llma-... token.
Route Purpose GET /admin/whoami the caller and their roles GET /admin/login, /admin/callback, /admin/session; POST /admin/logout administrator single sign-on (see Identity) GET, POST /admin/users; DELETE /admin/users/{name}; .../tokens; .../roles users, their tokens and their roles; names may contain @ and + GET, PUT /admin/allowlists IP allowlists on an organisation, a team or a key POST /admin/keys/{id}/rotate; PUT /admin/keys/{id}/rotation rotate a key’s secret now, or on a schedule /scim/v2 SCIM 2.0 provisioning, with a scim block GET, POST /admin/orgs; DELETE /admin/orgs/{name} organisations (one created here has no share: it only borrows) GET /admin/teams?org=, POST /admin/teams; DELETE /admin/teams/{name} teams GET, POST /admin/teams/{team}/projects; DELETE .../projects/{name} projects GET, PUT /admin/teams/{team}/models the model groups a team may use (empty list = every configured model) GET /admin/keys?team=, POST /admin/keys; DELETE /admin/keys/{id} keys (the llmf-... secret is returned once); a key may carry tags GET, PUT /admin/budgets; DELETE /admin/budgets?kind=&name=&model= budgets: {"kind","name","model","period","max_cost","soft_limit"} with period day, week or month POST /admin/budgets/increase a temporary increase with an expiry GET /admin/spend?from=&to=&group_by=&format= spend report grouped by any of org, team, project, key, model, pool, tag; json, csv or parsable2; filtered to what the caller may see GET /admin/usage.csv?from=&to= the v0.1 export GET /admin/fairshare reservations, in-flight, borrowing, usage, level fairshare and rank per pool and organisation A request is refused with 429, naming the scope, as soon as one budget it falls under is exhausted. soft_limit triggers one alert per budget and period, to a webhook and/or by e-mail through an SMTP relay.
data.admin-ui#Admin web UI:
With an sso block, /ui/ serves a web console for administrators (/admin/login?next=ui signs in and lands there). It is server-rendered HTML with no JavaScript, under a strict policy on every /ui/ response:
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; style-src 'self'; img-src 'self'; form-action 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'; base-uri 'none' plus X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, Referrer-Policy: no-referrer and Cache-Control: no-store. The one stylesheet is served by the gateway; no third-party asset is loaded.
Page What it does Keys list per team; create (the secret is shown once, on a page that is not cached), rotate with a grace period, revoke Budgets budgets with spent and limit; set and delete Spend GPU-hours, requests and tokens over a period, grouped by organisation, team, project, key, model, pool or tag Fair share live state per pool: reservation, in flight, borrowing, level fairshare and rank Audit entries page by page, and a button that verifies the chain (status of the checkpoints and of the anchor) The UI holds no privilege of its own: every page calls the admin API’s handlers in-process with the signed-in person, so it has the same RBAC as the API (an organisation administrator sees their organisation only) and every change is audited as through the API. Only an SSO session is accepted; without an sso block /ui/ answers 404. Two admin routes were added for it: GET /admin/audit?from=&limit= and POST /admin/audit/verify (proxy admins and viewers only). The verification uses the gateway’s own key; for an independent check use llmflow-gateway audit verify with a public key kept elsewhere (see Audit and logging).
data.architecture#Architecture: clients (OpenAI SDKs, Authorization: Bearer llmf-...) | v llmflow-gateway 1 auth: virtual key -> team (SHA-256, constant-time, cached) 2 body <= max_body_bytes, JSON re-encoded, client priority fields stripped, per-tenant cache_salt set 3 budget (GPU-hours per day / week / month), fail-closed by default 4 per-key RPM / TPM / max in-flight 5 fair share: within reservation -> priority 0/1, borrowing -> 10 and more 6 route: least in-flight healthy upstream, retry before the first byte 7 stream SSE event by event, capture usage 8 cost -> budget counter, fair-share usage, async PostgreSQL record | v headers built from scratch: Authorization (internal key), X-Vllm-Priority vLLM x N (--scheduling-policy priority --api-key ..., reachable only from the gateway) Packages: fairshare (the algorithm, no I/O), openai (request rewrite, SSE usage capture), store (memory and PostgreSQL), gateway (HTTP server), config, and cmd/llmflow-gateway (cobra command line).
data.configuration#Configuration (HCL2):
The configuration is written in HCL2 native syntax; the repository’s examples/gateway.hcl is parsed by its test suite, so it stays valid. This extract was run through llmflow-gateway check-config v0.8.0 (with the key files present):
master_key_file = "/etc/llmflow/master.key" cache_salt_key_file = "/etc/llmflow/cache-salt.key" org "etabA" { share = 0.8125 team "lab-nlp" {} team "lab-vision" {} } org "etabB" { share = 0.1875 team "lab-chem" {} } pool "b300" { capacity = 256 } model "llama-3.3-70b" { upstream_model = "meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct" pool = "b300" class = "interactive" key_file = "/etc/llmflow/vllm.key" cost { input_per_mtok = 0.02 output_per_mtok = 0.20 cached_per_mtok = 0.002 } upstream "gpu01" { base_url = "http://10.0.0.11:8000" } upstream "gpu02" { base_url = "http://10.0.0.12:8000" key_file = "/etc/llmflow/gpu02.key" } } Block or attribute Meaning org "" { share, team "" {} ... } an organisation (institution) with the fraction of every pool reserved for it (sum at most 1) and the teams declared under it; team names are global pool "" { capacity } C, the sustainable concurrency of the pool (1 to 1048576) model "" { ... } client model name; upstream_model, pool, class (interactive or batch), key_file, cost { input_per_mtok, output_per_mtok, cached_per_mtok } in GPU-hours per million tokens, and upstream "" { base_url, key_file } blocks store { ... } kind (memory or postgres), dsn_file, fail_closed (default true), queue_size, batch_size fairshare { half_life } usage decay half-life (default "168h") limits { ... }, health { ... } body and header sizes, timeouts, maximum request duration and response size; health-check interval, timeout, cooldown and path tags { header, allowed } the request header clients may tag requests with, and the allowed tags cache_isolation, cache_salt_key_file prefix-cache tenant scope (org default, team, key, none) and the HMAC key file (at least 32 bytes; required unless none) jwt { issuer, audience, type, rpm, map { claim, value, team, project } } OpenID Connect access tokens on the inference API; see Identity sso { issuer, client_id, client_secret_file, redirect_url, scopes, session_ttl, role { claim, value, role, team } } administrator single sign-on scim { token_file, base_url, group "" { team, role } } SCIM 2.0 provisioning vault { address, token_file, ca_file, namespace, cache_ttl }, key_rotation { vault_prefix, check_interval } OpenBao or Vault secret references (vault:/#), and scheduled key rotation trusted_proxies, routes { inference, admin, metrics, healthz { allow = [...] } } reverse proxies whose X-Forwarded-For is read, and the networks allowed per route class audit { signing_key_file, checkpoint_interval, anchor, anchor_max_lag, retention, prune_interval }, export "" { kind, endpoint, bucket, ... } the admin audit log and where its checkpoints, and the request logs, are exported; see Audit and logging logging "" { teams, destination, content, ... } per-team request logs; content is off by default policy "" { teams, require, require_tags, max_body_bytes, max_response_bytes } required fields and tags, and per-team or per-key size limits (POST /admin/keys {"policy"}) alerts { webhook_url, webhook_token_file, smtp { server, from, to, username, password_file } } where soft-budget alerts go auth_failures_per_minute failed authentications allowed per client network before a 429 (default 60, 0 disables) Design decisions of the format:
Static evaluation. The file is decoded with no evaluation context: no variables, no functions. env.HOME, file("/etc/shadow") or "${x}" are errors, so a configuration cannot read the environment or other files. Quoted strings are templates. A literal ${ must be written $${, and a literal %{ must be written %%{. This applies to every value, URLs, paths and model names included. Labelled blocks for named things: org, team, pool, model, upstream. Duplicate labels are errors. Teams nest inside their organisation. Every diagnostic carries file:line:column; check-config prints them one per line. Secrets only by file (master_key_file, metrics_token_file, store.dsn_file, key_file, cache_salt_key_file, and so on). An upstream URL with credentials is rejected. Durations are strings in Go syntax ("30s", "168h"). Absent and zero differ: retries = 0 disables retries, leaving it out takes the default. The parser is fuzzed (FuzzParse): the configuration is treated as untrusted input. Cost of a request, in GPU-hours: ((prompt - cached) x input + cached x cached_price + completion x output) / 10^6, from the usage vLLM reports.
data.fair-share-with-borrowing#How fair-share:
A pool has a capacity C: the concurrency it sustains without preemption, measured externally. Each organisation owns an integer reservation, shared by all its teams and projects, obtained by apportioning C over the shares with the largest-remainder (Hamilton) method, so reservations never sum to more than C (C = 256 gives A 208 and B 48).
For every request:
Situation Priority sent to vLLM the organisation has fewer within-share requests in flight than its reservation 0 interactive, 1 batch otherwise (borrowing) 10 + 10 x rank + class, rank at most 9 Among borrowers, rank is the dense rank of the organisation’s level fairshare LF = S / U (Slurm Fair Tree): the most under-served has rank 0, so the most over-served borrower gets the largest number, is admitted last and is preempted first. Usage is the cost actually consumed, charged when a request finishes and decayed with a half-life (the exact exponential, of which Slurm’s 1 - 0.693/hl is the first-order expansion).
vLLM’s v1 scheduler keeps waiting requests in a min-heap on (priority, arrival_time); when a running request runs out of KV blocks, the running request with the largest (priority, arrival_time) is preempted; a waiting request never preempts a running one. A within-share request is therefore admitted before any borrower and is never the victim while a borrower runs. The guide explains vLLM’s priority semantics from its source.
Two choices were forced by the simulator: the reservation test counts within-share requests in flight (not all requests), and usage is charged at release (not from time in flight, since a request waiting in vLLM’s queue consumes nothing).

data.fallbacks#Fallbacks:
A model group can name fallbacks, tried in order (at most 4, not a guard model, not itself):
model "llama-70b" { pool = "b300" fallbacks = ["llama-8b"] # ... } Before anything has reached the client, a request moves to the next fallback when no upstream of the group took it, or when vLLM answered 429 or 503. The target must be in the team’s model list and within its budgets. The request acquires in the target’s pool (so it gets its organisation’s priority there), is rewritten for the target, and is charged and recorded under the model that served it. The response carries X-Llmflow-Model, and llmflow_fallbacks_total{from,to} counts the moves. Any other answer, a 400 for instance, is final.
data.gateway#gateway: An OpenAI-compatible gateway in pure Go (CGO_ENABLED=0) that sits in front of vLLM on a GPU cluster shared by several institutions. It replaces LiteLLM for that role and adds fair-share scheduling with reservation and borrowing, mapped onto vLLM’s own priority scheduler. Repository →
data.hierarchy#Hierarchy and roles:
The tree mirrors a Slurm account tree: organisation (institution) → team (lab) → project → key. Budgets can be set on every scope (organisation, team, project, key, tag), and for one model group. Administration is delegated by role:
Role Scope May proxy_admin everything everything the master key may proxy_viewer everything read every listing, report and fair-share state org_admin one organisation manage its teams, projects, keys, budgets and users below it team_admin one team manage its projects and keys, grant member and viewer on the team member one team create keys (owned by the member), list and revoke their own keys viewer one organisation or team read its teams, projects, keys (no secrets), budgets and spend Users authenticate with admin tokens (llma-..., 256 random bits, stored as SHA-256, shown once). Nobody can grant a role above their own scope. Teams can restrict which model groups they may use.
data.limitations#Limitations:
Open defects of v0.8.0, as the repository lists them:
State is per process. In-flight counts, rate limits and the key cache live in memory: run one gateway replica per pool. Several replicas would each grant the full reservation. Budgets lag. The cost is known when a request ends, so a burst of long requests can overspend by what is in flight. Several gateways see each other’s spend only at their next refresh. Priority is fixed at admission. A borrowing request already queued in vLLM keeps its priority when its organisation drops back under its reservation, and teams inside an organisation share its reservation without sub-shares of their own. vLLM has no API to re-prioritise a queued request. Aborted requests are charged with an estimate (see above). Prefix-cache isolation is per scope, not absolute (see above). Accounting can drop records when its queue is full or a batch write fails twice (both are counted in metrics); budgets count the cost until the next refresh only. No TLS in the gateway: put it behind a TLS proxy. The admin API shares the client listener. /v1/responses is served statelessly only (see above). C is static configuration; the gateway does not measure or adapt it. Admin principals are read from the store on every admin request, with no cache: role changes apply at once, but the admin API fails with the store. Soft-budget alert retries live in memory. Each channel (webhook, SMTP) is retried on its own, up to 6 attempts with exponential backoff; a 4xx other than 408 and 429 is not retried; every webhook attempt carries the same Idempotency-Key. A gateway stopped mid-retry does not resume: the period is already marked as alerted. SSO sessions live in one replica’s memory: behind several replicas, use sticky sessions. A person holding a JWT cannot be revoked individually: disable the team, change the map blocks, or revoke at the identity provider; a token already verified stays cached until its exp or key_cache_ttl. SCIM does not expand nested groups, and a provisioned role on a team that does not exist is logged, not created. The audit log’s guarantees end at its newest anchor. Without an anchor export, truncation, rollback and deletion of the database go undetected; with one, what happened after the newest exported checkpoint can still be removed, and a stolen signing key can sign new history after it. Keep the key in OpenBao or Vault, verify with a public key kept elsewhere, and keep an anchor on write-once storage. See the threat model. What guardrails do not inspect. Streamed tool-call arguments cannot be masked, so a guarded stream that carries them is stopped (ask without stream). Reasoning text, refusals, log probabilities and unknown fields are removed from guarded answers, not inspected. A secret whose start appears more than 256 bytes before it can match is not seen in a stream, and a span still open after 64 KiB is released masked only as far as it has reached. Guardrail audit entries are written asynchronously and dropped, counted and alerted when the queue is full. A Responses stream under post-call guardrails is refused. Phone numbers have no checksum: a PII guardrail that masks them also masks 10-digit references that start with 0. The performance of v0.6 and v0.7 is not measured yet. The overhead figures are those of v0.1.0; an independent benchmark of the current release is waiting for a quiet machine.
data.mcp#MCP gateway:
POST /mcp is an MCP server in front of the tool servers of the configuration. It speaks the Streamable HTTP binding of revision 2026-07-28 and, for older clients, the initialize handshake of 2025-11-25 (and 2025-06-18, 2025-03-26). A client authenticates with its virtual key. This block passes llmflow-gateway check-config v0.8.0 (with the key files present, and an sso block, organisations, a pool and a model around it):
mcp_server "github" { url = "https://mcp.example.org/github/mcp" token_file = "/etc/llmflow/mcp-github.token" protocol = "2026-07-28" timeout = "60s" max_response_bytes = 8388608 } Tools are named .. Per-team allow-lists, closed by default. A team with no list sees no tool. An organisation administrator sets it with PUT /admin/teams/{team}/tools {"tools":["github.*","docs.search"]} (a pattern is *, .* or ., and must name a configured server). Team administrators can read the list but cannot widen it. A call to any other tool answers -32602 Unknown tool, like a tool that does not exist, and the refusal is audited (tool.denied). Every call is audited before it is made. A tool.call entry names the key, its organisation, team and project, the tool, and the SHA-256 and size of the arguments; the arguments are hashed, never stored. If that entry cannot be written, the call is not made (503). A tool.result entry follows with the outcome. llmflow_tool_calls_total{team,server,status} counts the calls, and the audit retention accepts the kind tool. Only configured servers are reached. Clients name tools, never URLs; the gateway sends requests only to the url of an mcp_server block, follows no redirect, uses no environment proxy and never fetches what a server returns. The tool servers’ tokens come from the secret source and the client’s key is never forwarded. Tool calls count against the key’s RPM and in-flight limits and cost no GPU-hours. Not covered: OAuth 2.1 discovery (virtual keys are static bearer tokens), resources and prompts, guardrails on tool arguments and results, and SSE toward MCP clients.
data.messages#Anthropic Messages API: POST /v1/messages is proxied to vLLM’s own Anthropic endpoint, with no translation in the gateway, so coding agents that speak the Messages API can use local models. A virtual key is the bearer token. Guardrails cover system, text and thinking blocks, tool_result content and every string inside tool_use inputs; blocks they cannot read (a document) are refused. Guarded streams pass through an Anthropic event filter. Errors carry both OpenAI’s {"error": ...} and Anthropic’s top-level "type": "error". /v1/messages/count_tokens is not routed.
data.more-endpoints#More endpoints: All of these go through the same pipeline as chat: authentication, policies, budgets, rate limits, guardrails, fair-share priority and the tenant’s cache_salt.
data.overhead#Overhead:
An independent A/B against LiteLLM, measured on 2026-10-23.
Protocol. A Go tool, gwbench, with tests; its control test sees a planted 3 ms delay. Requests go one at a time, the order of the targets is randomised at every round, and the overhead is paired round by round against a direct call to the same fake upstream.
Targets. LiteLLM 1.106.2 (one process, no database) and llmflow v0.1.0 (GOMAXPROCS=1, memory store), on a small non-streaming request.
Load. Each run of 2,000 rounds starts only at a 1-minute load of 4 or less, and is discarded if the load ends above 4. A first long run was discarded (the load rose to 9.44). Eight runs were kept, at loads 3.30 to 3.94.
Result, over 16,000 paired rounds:
Overhead p50 p90 p99 LiteLLM 4.86 ms 5.26 ms 6.21 ms llmflow 117 us 161 us 239 us That is about 40 times lower at the median and 26 times at p99. The per-run median varied from 4.84 to 4.93 ms for LiteLLM and from 115 to 120 us for llmflow.
What it does not measure. No streaming, no concurrency, and no database write: the gateway ran with its memory store. These are to be measured on the cluster.
data.prefix-cache-isolation#Prefix-cache isol:
Why. vLLM reuses cached KV blocks across requests that share a prompt prefix. That reuse is a timing side channel: a caller can test whether a guessed prefix is already cached by measuring the time to first token, and so learn what another tenant sent. vLLM’s security guide documents it, and it is tracked as CVE-2025-46570. On a cluster shared by several institutions this is a leak between institutions.
What the gateway does. It removes any cache_salt the client sends and always sets its own: base64url(HMAC-SHA256(key, scope)), 43 characters (256 bits). The key is read from cache_salt_key_file, and the scope is set by cache_isolation:
cache_isolation One prefix cache per org (default) organisation (institution) team team key virtual key none nothing: a single tenant vLLM mixes the salt into the hash of the first KV block and every later block chains from it, so different scopes never share cached blocks. The salt is stable per scope (a random salt per request would disable prefix caching). Multimodal uuid values in the message content parts are rewritten per tenant, not stripped: a client can keep referring to media it sent earlier, while the same uuid sent by two tenants names two different cache entries.
Operating it. cache_salt_key_file must hold at least 32 random bytes and be readable by its owner only (mode 0600); it is mandatory unless cache_isolation = "none". Rotating the key means a cold prefix cache for everyone.
Residual risk. Within one scope the cache is shared. With the default org, users of the same institution can still probe each other by timing; team or key narrow that, at the cost of less cache reuse. And vLLM itself states that cache_salt is not an isolation boundary: tenants that need hard isolation need a vLLM instance of their own.
data.rerank#Rerank, tokenization, audio: POST /v1/rerank and /v2/rerank serve score models; they are guarded and charged on the usage’s prompt tokens. POST /tokenize and /detokenize are authenticated and rate limited but not charged and not guarded: no model runs, and masking would make the count wrong. POST /v1/audio/transcriptions takes a bounded multipart form, rebuilt from an allow-list of fields before it is forwarded. The file is limited by limits { max_audio_bytes } (25 MiB by default), and a model is charged with cost { audio_per_hour } in GPU-hours per hour of audio. The audio itself is not inspected, and the content log never holds it. A client chat_template is stripped from every request.
data.responses#Responses API: stateless only:
POST /v1/responses is proxied to vLLM’s own Responses endpoint. The gateway forces "store": false and refuses previous_response_id, background, conversation and a stored prompt with a 400 that says so. GET /v1/responses/{id} and the cancel route are not routed. Clients send the whole conversation in input, as with chat completions.
Why. vLLM keeps every response in the memory of the instance that produced it (store defaults to true there). Anyone holding the id can read it back, continue it or cancel it. Behind a gateway that state would be shared by every tenant and would live on one upstream among several, so a tenant holding an id could read or continue another tenant’s conversation.
Usage is read from the Responses usage, including the final response.completed event of a stream. Guardrails read instructions and the input items; input items they cannot read are refused. A streamed Responses request under post-call guardrails is refused (400; ask with "stream": false).
data.roadmap#Roadmap:
Issue #7 tracks shipping every LiteLLM Enterprise feature in the open-source gateway. M1 (governance and multi-tenancy) is done, in v0.2.0, M2 (identity and access) in v0.4.0, and M3 (audit and logging) in v0.5.0, and M4 (guardrails) in v0.6.0. The version numbers written in the issue shifted by one when v0.3.0 was taken by the security patch.
A further milestone, issue #38 (“M5”), covers more endpoints and operations. Its first five items shipped in v0.7.0 (the endpoints, fallbacks and tracing described above), and the last two, the admin web UI and the MCP gateway, in v0.8.0. Issue #38 is closed and M5 is complete.
data.routes#Routes: Client routes: POST /v1/chat/completions, /v1/completions, /v1/embeddings, /v1/responses (stateless only), /v1/messages (Anthropic Messages API), /v1/rerank, /v2/rerank, /v1/audio/transcriptions, /tokenize, /detokenize, and GET /v1/models. Also GET /healthz, which returns 503 when the budget state is stale and fail-closed is on, and GET /metrics (Prometheus text format, optional bearer token). All are described under More endpoints; how coding agents use them is on the Coding agents page.
data.security#Security: Clients cannot choose their priority. The body is parsed and re-encoded (duplicate keys and escaped spellings cannot survive); priority, extra_body, request_id, kv_transfer_params, ec_transfer_params and vllm_xargs are removed. Upstream headers are built from scratch, so a client’s X-Vllm-Priority, x-pass-*, Authorization and X-Forwarded-* never reach vLLM. This closes a hole measured on LiteLLM. The rewrite and the SSE copier are fuzzed (FuzzRewrite, FuzzCopySSE). vLLM must only be reachable from the gateway. Its --api-key covers only /v1, /v2 and /inference; /invocations exposes inference without authentication. Firewall the vLLM ports (guide). Identity (v0.4.0). OpenID Connect access tokens are verified by go-authn/oidc (no alg: none, no HMAC, aud and exp required, https key fetches rate-limited), administrator sessions use a __Host- cookie with CSRF token and Origin check, and every refusal on the inference API is the same 401. X-Forwarded-For is read from the right and only from trusted_proxies; routes can be restricted to networks; IP allowlists must all match. Details on the Identity page. Audit (v0.5.0). Admin actions are in a hash-chained log with signed checkpoints, which an anchor on write-once storage makes hard to rewrite. What stays open is stated on the Audit and logging page. Keys. Virtual keys and admin tokens are 256-bit random secrets, stored as SHA-256, compared in constant time and shown once. Secrets come from files only and never appear in logs, errors or listings. No SSRF. Upstreams come from the configuration only; client input selects a model group, never a URL. Upstream redirects are not followed. Brute force. Failed authentications are limited per client network (IPv4 address or IPv6 /64, from the connection, not from proxy headers) by auth_failures_per_minute; valid and missed keys live in two separate bounded caches, so a spray of random keys cannot evict valid ones. Limits on body, headers, timeouts, request duration and upstream response size; a bounded accounting queue. Budgets fail closed: when PostgreSQL cannot be read for 3 refresh periods, every request gets 503 (fail_closed = false to fail open). CI: race tests on amd64 and arm64, PostgreSQL integration tests, fuzz smoke, govulncheck, CGO_ENABLED=0 cross-builds.

data.fair-share#Fair-share on a co-owned GPU:
How to share four HGX B300 servers (32 GPUs) between two institutions, A and B, with Slurm for batch computing, vLLM for inference, a gateway for keys and quotas, and VS Code to reach it all. The sharing must respect each institution’s share and leave no GPU idle.
This is an English adaptation of a design and operations document, version 1.1 of 23 October 2026. Every parameter cited refers to the vendors’ documentation consulted on that date (see the bibliography). The measurements are real and dated: they were made on LiteLLM 1.106.2 on 23 October 2026.
The guide has three layers, one page each:
Slurm guarantees each institution its share (QOS caps, preemption of borrowing jobs) and divides the rest by fair-share (the Fair Tree algorithm): Slurm. vLLM serves the language models in long Slurm jobs, and a gateway in front of it authenticates users, applies per-institution quotas and counts consumption in tokens: Inference. One accounting, in GPU-hours, ties the two: Accounting. Then VS Code access, identity with your federation (RENATER, eduGAIN), the security audit, acceptance tests and governance, and the bibliography.
data.hardware#The hardware:
Each server is an HGX B300 with 8 Blackwell Ultra SXM GPUs linked by NVLink 5. Figures are NVIDIA’s (the HGX datasheet, the Blackwell Ultra technical blog and the DGX B300 user guide).
per GPU per server (8 GPUs) HBM3e memory 288 GB 2.3 TB (8 x 288); 2.1 TB on the HGX datasheet HBM bandwidth 8 TB/s – NVLink 5, GPU to GPU (bidirectional) 1.8 TB/s 14.4 TB/s in total NVFP4, dense / sparse 15 / 20 PFLOPS 108 / 144 PFLOPS FP8, dense / sparse 5 / 10 PFLOPS 36 / 72 PFLOPS FP64 – 10 TFLOPS INT8 (sparse) – 3 POPS (72 on HGX B200) MIG partitions up to 7 instances (for example 7 x 34 GB) – Power TGP up to 1,400 W DGX B300: 14.5 kW, 15 kW max Per-GPU and per-server figures are not always in a ratio of 8: 108/8 = 13.5 PFLOPS rather than 15, and 2.1 TB rather than 8 x 288 GB. NVIDIA states that memory and SM count vary by part number. Use the values of your vendor’s datasheet. As an example, the DGX B300 has 2 Xeon Platinum 6776P and 2 TB of RAM (up to 4).
The B300 is an AI machine, not a double-precision scientific one. 10 TFLOPS of FP64 for 8 GPUs, and an INT8 rate divided by 24 relative to the B200. A classic FP64 code (CFD, quantum chemistry, finite elements) wastes its institution’s share here. The agreement between the institutions should say so; such codes belong on other facilities. The cluster has 32 GPUs. A practical consequence: a model served with tensor parallelism 8 (--tensor-parallel-size 8) occupies a whole server, because NVLink does not connect two servers.
data.hybrid#The hybrid model in one sentence:
By default each institution submits to its own owner QOS, capped at its share; those jobs are never preempted. Beyond its share it submits to the borrow QOS, uncapped but preemptible by the owner QOS. Among waiting jobs, the order depends on fair-share, which penalises the institution that consumed more than its share over the last two weeks.
VS Code ──HTTPS──> gateway (keys, teams, quotas, accounting) ──internal──> vLLM (Continue, (Slurm jobs, Remote-SSH) QOS service) └──SSH──> login node (sbatch, srun) ──> slurmctld + slurmdbd ──> gpu01 ... gpu04 (Fair Tree, QOS, preemption) 4 x 8 B300
data.objectives#Objectives: Guarantee: each institution gets its share (26 or 6 GPUs) within a bounded, known delay, even when the cluster is full. No loss: a GPU its owner does not use is lent to the other institution. Fairness over time: over a sliding window, each one’s consumption tends to its share. Whoever borrowed a lot goes behind the other. One accounting: batch and inference are both read in GPU-hours, for re-invoicing and governance. Security: GPU isolation between jobs, and no inference service reachable without authentication.
data.ownership#Ownership:
Institution A bought 3 whole servers and the remaining quarter of the 4th; institution B bought the other three quarters of the 4th. If a later purchase changes the split, update this table and the values derived from it (Fairshare, GrpTRES).
Institution Servers GPUs Share Slurm Fairshare A 3 + 1/4 26 81.25 % 26 B 3/4 6 18.75 % 6 Total 4 32 100 % 32 Slurm shares are expressed in GPUs, which keeps them readable. Slurm normalises against siblings (S = S_self / S_(self+siblings)), so only the ratio 26:6 counts.

data.accounting#One accounting:
Batch is counted in GPU-equivalent hours (sreport, after TRESBillingWeights). Inference is counted in tokens, per team (the gateway’s spend logs). They are reconciled as follows:
Over the period (a month), read the GPU-hours of the svc_llm account: H_svc. Read each team’s spend in the gateway: D_A, D_B. Charge H_svc x D_A / (D_A + D_B) to A, and the remainder to B. Compare each institution’s total consumption (batch plus charged inference) with its share (81.25 % / 18.75 %).
data.calibration#Calibrating the internal cos:
Goal: 1 unit of gateway spend = 1 GPU-hour. A saturated 8-GPU instance then “spends” 8 units per hour, and max_budget becomes a quota of inference GPU-hours, directly comparable with batch.
1. Measure the capacity. Once per model and per configuration (TP, KV-cache dtype), with vllm bench serve [24]. Use a mix of lengths representative of the real usage (for example 2,000 input tokens and 300 output tokens for a code assistant). Raise --max-concurrency up to the limit of the service target, for instance a p99 time to first token under 2 s:
vllm bench serve --backend openai-chat --endpoint /v1/chat/completions \ --host gpu01.internal --port 8000 --model \ --dataset-name random --random-input-len 2000 --random-output-len 300 \ --num-prompts 2000 --max-concurrency 64 --save-result At the chosen concurrency C (which also serves the fair-share relay), read the output throughput T_out and the total throughput T_tot in tokens/s, printed by the tool [24]. The input throughput is T_in = T_tot - T_out.
2. Split the cost of an instance-hour. Prefill (input) costs much less per token than generation. Fix a ratio r = c_out / c_in, typically r = 4, and solve:
3600 (c_in T_in + c_out T_out) = 8 => c_in = 8 / (3600 (T_in + r T_out)), c_out = r c_in A fictitious example, to illustrate the computation (the real figures come out of step 1): T_in = 40,000, T_out = 6,000 tokens/s, r = 4. Then c_in = 8 / (3600 x 64,000) = 3.5e-8 and c_out = 1.4e-7 unit per token.
3. Tokens served from the prefix cache. LiteLLM warns that a model with custom pricing bills these tokens at 0 as long as cache_read_input_token_cost is not set (a warning observed at LiteLLM 1.106.2 start-up). Set it to about c_in / 10: these tokens are not recomputed, but they occupy KV memory.
Why not a cost per second? LiteLLM accepts cost_per_second [22]. But vLLM processes dozens of requests simultaneously on one instance: billing each by its duration would make it pay for the whole instance, and the sum would far exceed the real 8 GPU-hours. The per-token cost is the right model.
Recalibrate at each change of model, vLLM version or KV-cache dtype, and check once a month. The GPU-hours of the svc_llm account read from sreport should stay close to the month’s total gateway spend divided by the average occupancy.
data.compensation#Compensation: If, over a quarter, an institution consumed markedly more than its share through inference, the committee may correct the Slurm Fairshare values of the next quarter. Batch fair-share already rebalances by itself within the half-life window: compensation is only an exceptional adjustment.

data.acceptance#Acceptance tests: prove the g:
Every guarantee is proven by a test that could fail:
B’s guarantee. A fills the 32 GPUs (13 in instA, 19 in borrow). B submits 3 GPUs in instB. Measure the start delay: it must stay under 36 minutes, and under 6 minutes if the borrowed jobs are older than 30 minutes. Negative control. The same scenario with the borrow QOS without Preempt: B must wait. If B starts anyway, test 1 was not measuring preemption. Cap. B submits 8 GPUs in instB: immediate rejection (DenyOnLimit). Fair-share. After a week in which B borrows heavily, sshare -l must show LF_B < 1, and A’s borrow jobs must go ahead of B’s (sprio). Billing. A job of 1 GPU and 64 cores must be billed 4: the billing= field of AllocTRES in sacct. Inference. Saturate the model with a key of A; check that a key of B still gets about 18.75 % of the throughput (with the Enterprise reservation, or the relay) or its static limit. vLLM priority. During saturation, a request of the large-model group (priority 0) must have a time to first token markedly lower than a request of large-model-batch (priority 10). Inviolable priority. Send to large-model-batch a request with extra_body: {"priority": 0} and a header X-Vllm-Priority: 0. It must stay processed at priority 10. Control: the same request sent directly to vLLM goes ahead. B’s window. One hour before instB_weekly opens, submit in borrow a 3 h job and a 30 min job. Only the second must start on the reserved server. At opening, an 8-GPU job of B must start immediately. Performance. Compare throughput (tokens/s) and latency (time to first token, p50/p99) of vLLM behind the gateway with those of vLLM direct, at equal load. The gateway’s overhead must stay negligible next to generation; if it does not, increase the number of gateway workers before touching vLLM.
data.governance#Governance: Agreement between institutions: shares (26/6), guaranteed delay (36 min), size of the inference pool, half-life (14 days), the quarterly compensation rule, and the possible reservation of a whole server for B. Quarterly technical committee: real consumption against share, median wait times per institution and per QOS, preemption rate, inference saturation. Change of shares (the purchase of a 5th server, say): change the Fairshare and GrpTRES values. No redeployment is needed.
data.security-audit#Security audit:
Surface Risk Measure Shared GPUs a job reads the GPU memory of another institution ConstrainDevices=yes [7]; no shard between institutions [5] vLLM unauthenticated endpoints outside /v1 [10] internal listening only; firewall: only the gateway reaches it Gateway quota bypass during a Redis/DB outage [11] fail-closed options; Redis and Postgres made redundant Gateway budgets inoperative on a zero-cost model [11] non-zero internal cost (accounting) Keys leak through a URL, a command line or an environment variable files with mode 0600; Continue secrets; rotation; one key per use Logs confidential prompts stored in the database disable message-content logging; keep only spend metadata vLLM prefix cache timing side channel between institutions: a caller detects a cached prefix by its time to first token (CVE-2025-46570) per-tenant cache_salt set by the gateway (prefix-cache isolation); a vLLM instance per tenant if hard isolation is needed Login node computation outside Slurm per-user cgroup limits; SSH access to GPU nodes reserved to jobs Preemption loss of work of borrowed jobs GraceTime plus checkpoint; PreemptExemptTime vLLM priority a client gives itself priority 0 through extra_body (measured, measurements) priority pinned by header; client-header forwarding disabled; the relay (or the Go gateway) overwrites Header forwarding the client’s x-pass-* and x-* reach vLLM if forwarding is on [23] leave forward_client_headers_to_llm_api disabled FP64 usage double-precision codes on B300 (10 TFLOPS per server) [12] usage rule in the agreement Audit anchor. The Go gateway (audit log since v0.5.0) keeps a hash-chained audit log of every administrative change, with signed checkpoints. A log in the database that the operator can edit is only partly trustworthy: deploy the audit anchor on the same S3 or Ceph storage the cluster already has, in a bucket created with Object Lock, so that exported checkpoints cannot be deleted or rewritten, and check the log with llmflow-gateway audit verify --anchor export and a public key kept outside the operators’ reach. Without an anchor, truncation and rollback go undetected. The Audit and logging page states what remains open.
Guardrails (gateway v0.6.0). Prompts and completions can be checked before and after vLLM, on this cluster, without sending them anywhere: hide_secrets masks tokens and URL credentials (using gitsafe’s redact), pii masks or blocks personal data (e-mail, phone, IBAN, French NIR, cards, IP addresses) with go-llmflow/pii, and llama_guard and prompt_guard classify with a Llama Guard or Prompt Guard model served locally by vLLM on the cluster, as a model of class guard that clients cannot call. The classifiers see the already-masked text. A guardrail that errs or times out refuses (503) by default. The generic HTTP adapter is off by default: it exists only when written, and then only with allow_external = true, because it sends prompts and completions out of the site. This block passes check-config v0.8.0:
guardrail "secrets" { type = "hide_secrets" orgs = ["instA", "instB"] } guardrail "pii" { type = "pii" teams = ["b-lab"] action = "mask" actions = { iban = "block", nir = "block", phone = "log" } } guardrail "safety" { type = "llama_guard" model = "llama-guard" teams = ["b-lab"] action = "block" timeout = "2s" on_error = "block" } model "llama-guard" { upstream_model = "meta-llama/Llama-Guard-3-8B" pool = "guard" class = "guard" key_file = "/etc/llmflow/vllm.key" upstream "g0" { base_url = "http://gpu09:8000" } } (Alongside the organisations, teams, the pool "guard" and the other models.)
Chaos to play during acceptance. Kill a vLLM instance under sustained traffic (the routing must fail over); cut Redis (the fail-closed mode must answer 503, not let requests through); preempt a borrowed job in the middle of writing a checkpoint (the resume must read the last complete checkpoint); restart slurmdbd during a mass submission.

data.bridge#1. Register the gateway at the br:
The gateway is a client of the bridge. This block is authn-bridge’s configuration, copied from the gateway’s README (it is not llmflow-gateway configuration, so check-config does not apply to it):
client "llmflow-admin" { secret_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/llmflow-admin.secret" redirect_uris = ["https://llm.example.org/admin/callback"] id_token_claims = true # the bridge's ID tokens carry no claims about the person otherwise }
data.gateway#2. Point the gateway’s sso and j:
Administrators log in through sso; users of the inference API present the access token through jwt. The groups the bridge returns are entitlements held to the institution that asserted them, so the role and map blocks match them. This block was run through llmflow-gateway check-config v0.8.0 (with the key files present, and organisations, a pool and a model alongside):
master_key_file = "/etc/llmflow/master.key" cache_salt_key_file = "/etc/llmflow/cache-salt.key" sso { issuer = "https://bridge.example.org" client_id = "llmflow-admin" client_secret_file = "/etc/llmflow/sso.secret" redirect_url = "https://llm.example.org/admin/callback" scopes = ["openid", "profile", "groups"] role { value = "llm-admins" role = "proxy_admin" } role { value = "b-lab-leads" role = "team_admin" team = "b-lab" } } jwt { issuer = "https://bridge.example.org" audience = "llmflow" type = "at+jwt" map { value = "b-lab" team = "b-lab" } } With this, a member of B’s laboratory who holds a token with the group b-lab reaches the gateway as a person of team b-lab: their requests count in B’s share, their budget and limits are the team’s, and the spend report names them. The value strings stand for whatever entitlements your federation really issues (for example urn:mace:... values); read them from a real token before writing the blocks.
Behind it, the gateway refuses alg: none and HMAC tokens, requires aud and exp, and answers every refusal with the same 401. See the Identity page for the details, for SCIM provisioning and for key rotation, and keep in mind its limitations: a person holding a token cannot be revoked individually before it expires, and SSO sessions live in one replica.
data.identity#Identity with your federation:
On a cluster co-owned by two institutions, people already have an account at their own institution. The aim is that nobody needs a second one: A’s and B’s users log in where they always do, and the gateway learns from that login which team they belong to.
If the institutions are in a SAML federation such as RENATER (France) or eduGAIN, the piece in the middle is authn-bridge (go-authn/bridge): an OpenID Connect provider placed in front of the federation. People log in at their own university; the gateway, which speaks OpenID Connect, gets a token. The bridge and the libraries below are documented in go-authn’s repositories; this page only shows how the gateway is pointed at them.
user ──> their university (SAML, RENATER / eduGAIN) │ v authn-bridge (OpenID Connect provider) │ token v llmflow gateway: sso (administrators), jwt (inference API) ──> vLLM
